passage:
Friday, 9 June
Result came at 11. I cleared the bank PO exam. Rank 212. Papa cried on the phone, Mummy distributed sweets to the whole lane. Gopika sent fifteen party poppers. 🎉
So why am I sitting here at midnight feeling nothing?
Two years of coaching. Two years of skipping cousins' weddings and the photography club. Papa's dream since I was in Class 8: "a secure bank job, like Sharma uncle's daughter." I said it so often I thought it was mine.
Today I opened my old camera bag, the one I haven't touched since first year. The lens was dusty. I cleaned it for an hour and felt more doing that than I did when the result came.
I don't know what to do with that.
Sangeeta

qa.q: What rank did Sangeeta get in the bank PO exam?
qa.a: Rank 212.

qa.q: Why might Sangeeta feel nothing at midnight after clearing the exam?
qa.a: Sangeeta may feel empty because the goal was Papa's dream, repeated so often it seemed like Sangeeta's own, so reaching it didn't touch what Sangeeta actually values.

qa.q: What turning point does the dusty camera offer Sangeeta?
qa.a: Cleaning the lens stirred more feeling than the result; Sangeeta could make time for photography again and think honestly about next steps before deciding anything big.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if he read this diary entry?
qa.a: Papa, who cried with joy, might be confused and hurt, but could also begin to see that the dream he chose wasn't the one his child held.

grounding: In a diary, a young adult reaches a family-set target and feels empty because it never matched personal values.

passage: When the letter came from the district office, half the village seemed to arrive in Chandrika's courtyard. She had cleared the constable exam, the first girl from their Punjab village to do it. Her father made everyone sit on charpais for tea. Her uncle made a speech about honour. Chandrika smiled for every photo. Late that night her cousin Amandeep found her by the cowshed, staring at the vegetable beds she had planted: tomatoes, okra, three kinds of chilli. "You're not happy," Amandeep said. Chandrika pulled a weed. "Everyone wanted this so much. I kept running because they were cheering. Now I've arrived, and I only feel tired." She looked at the chillies. "These make me happier than that letter."

qa.q: What had Chandrika planted in the vegetable beds?
qa.a: Tomatoes, okra, and three kinds of chilli.

qa.q: Why does Chandrika only feel tired after clearing the exam?
qa.a: She ran toward a goal the family cheered for rather than one she chose, so arriving brought no real satisfaction.

qa.q: What choice could Chandrika make now, without rushing?
qa.a: She could talk honestly with Amandeep, and later her father, about what she values, like the vegetable beds, before deciding how to shape her future.

qa.q: How might Chandrika's father see the letter compared with Chandrika?
qa.a: For him it means pride and honour for the family; for Chandrika it is the end of someone else's race.

grounding: A young woman in a village achieves the exam goal her family set and feels empty, drawn instead to what she values.

passage:
The graduation party at Tuan's parents' house in Melbourne was loud: aunties, cousins, a huge tray of spring rolls, and a banner his mother had printed: FIRST CLASS HONOURS! ACCOUNTING!
Tuan smiled for every photo. It was the result his dad had talked about since Tuan was fourteen, and he'd hit it exactly.
Later, Daniel found him on the back step, a plate going cold on his knees.
'You did it, man. Why do you look like you lost something?'
Tuan turned the paper plate slowly. 'I kept thinking that when I got here, I'd feel... done. Happy. I just feel like I finished someone else's homework.'
Inside, his dad was telling the story of the results email for the third time.
'What would have felt like yours?' Daniel asked.
Tuan didn't answer. He was looking at the vegetable garden he'd been planting with his grandmother every weekend for years.

qa.q: What did the banner Tuan's mother printed say?
qa.a: FIRST CLASS HONOURS! ACCOUNTING!

qa.q: Why does Tuan feel empty after reaching the goal?
qa.a: The target had been his dad's since Tuan was fourteen, not something he valued himself; reaching it felt like finishing 'someone else's homework'.

qa.q: What question could become a turning point for Tuan, and why?
qa.a: Daniel's 'What would have felt like yours?'; it invites Tuan to look at his own values, perhaps the garden he tends with his grandmother, instead of borrowed targets.

qa.q: How might Tuan's dad see the day, compared with Tuan?
qa.a: His dad is proud and happy, retelling the results email; he probably has no idea Tuan feels empty, since to him the goal was a gift.

grounding: A young man reaches the degree result his family set for him and feels empty, because the goal was never his own.

passage:
The hostel common room at the engineering college erupted when the warden read out the result: 'General Secretary, Jatin Rathore, 212 votes.' Jatin's wing lifted him onto their shoulders, chanting.
It had been Ramesh's idea since first year. 'You'll be GS, bro. Our wing needs a GS.' Ramesh made the posters, planned the speeches and counted votes in his head for weeks.
That night, after the sweets and the selfies, Jatin sat alone in the empty mess, the victory garland on the table beside him.
He had wanted this, hadn't he? He'd said so a hundred times. So why did it feel like a costume?
What he had really enjoyed all year was Saturday evenings teaching maths to the canteen workers' children, which nobody had voted for.
Ramesh came in. 'GS! Why are you sitting here in the dark?'

qa.q: How many votes did Jatin get?
qa.a: 212 votes.

qa.q: Why did the win feel like a costume to Jatin?
qa.a: The goal came from Ramesh and the wing, not from what Jatin valued; he had said he wanted it so often that he never checked, and reaching it left him empty.

qa.q: What choice could Jatin make now that he has noticed where he felt most alive?
qa.a: Jatin could put real energy into the Saturday maths classes, perhaps using the post to support them; linking the role to what he values might make it feel like his own.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel on finding Jatin alone in the dark?
qa.a: Ramesh, who worked for years on this win, would likely be confused and a little hurt, not realising the goal was mostly his own.

grounding: A student wins a hostel election his friends set as his goal and feels hollow, since his real interest lay elsewhere.

passage: The acceptance letter from the accounting firm in Osaka arrived on a Tuesday, and by Friday Hiroshi's father had booked a table at the family's favourite restaurant. It was the firm his father had talked about since Hiroshi was twelve. Hiroshi had studied for it for four years, turned down a summer at a pottery studio for it, practised the interviews in the mirror. Now, at the table, his uncles raised their glasses. Hiroshi smiled and raised his. Inside, he felt nothing. Not joy, not relief. Just a flat quiet, like a room after the guests have left. Later, walking home with his friend Thabo, he said, 'I thought I'd feel something.' Thabo asked, 'Did you want it, or did you want them to be happy?' Hiroshi didn't answer. He was thinking, oddly, about the smell of wet clay.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi turn down for the firm?
qa.a: He turned down a summer at a pottery studio.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi feel nothing at the celebration?
qa.a: He had reached a goal set by his father, not one that matched his own values, so instead of joy he felt flat and empty.

qa.q: What could Hiroshi do with Thabo's question?
qa.a: He could reflect honestly on what he values, perhaps the pottery, and look for ways to bring it into his life and future choices.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi's father feel at the table?
qa.a: His father probably felt proud and joyful, seeing a long-held hope come true, unaware that Hiroshi felt empty.

grounding: A young man reaches the job his father always wanted for him and feels empty, because the goal was never his own.

passage: The convocation hall at the university in Jaipur was packed, and when they called 'Himani, gold medal, B.Sc. Chemistry', her parents stood up and cheered. Himani walked to the stage, bowed, and felt the medal settle on her neck. She had worked three years for this. Her mother had talked of the gold since the first semester; her friends had bet on it. Back in her seat, she waited for the happiness. It didn't come. Vasudha, beside her, squeezed her hand. 'You did it!' 'I did,' Himani said. She looked at the medal. It looked like someone else's. What she kept remembering, strangely, was last summer's volunteering at the village school, teaching children to grow bean sprouts in cotton wool, and how she had laughed all day. 'Why do I feel so empty?' she whispered. Vasudha didn't know what to say.

qa.q: What medal did Himani receive?
qa.a: She received the gold medal in B.Sc. Chemistry.

qa.q: Why did Himani feel empty after winning the gold medal?
qa.a: The gold was her mother's and friends' goal, not one tied to what she truly values, so achieving it brought little satisfaction.

qa.q: What might Himani learn from remembering the village school?
qa.a: That teaching children brought her real joy, so she could explore goals built around that rather than borrowed targets.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel hearing 'Why do I feel so empty?'
qa.a: Vasudha is likely confused and a little worried, since she expected her friend to be thrilled.

grounding: A student wins the gold medal her family and friends expected and feels empty, because the goal did not match her own values.

passage:
Dear Pema,
I cleared it. The state services prelims, first attempt. Everyone at home has been calling since morning. Papa distributed sweets in the whole lane. My friends from coaching say I'm a legend.
And I'm sitting here in my room feeling like I've climbed the wrong hill.
You know I only started this because everyone in our town said a government job is the only real success. My cousins, my coaching group, Papa. I never really asked myself what I wanted. I just ran. Now that I've arrived, it's quiet. No fireworks inside.
The only time this year I felt truly alive was the week I helped the NGO map the lake's birds. You were there. You saw.
I don't know what to do with this. Tell me honestly if I'm being ungrateful.
Naveen

qa.q: Which exam did Naveen clear?
qa.a: Naveen cleared the state services prelims, first attempt.

qa.q: What does Naveen mean by 'climbed the wrong hill'?
qa.a: Naveen feels empty and confused, because the goal came from the town, family and friends rather than from Naveen's own values.

qa.q: How could Pema help Naveen think this through?
qa.a: Pema could reassure Naveen that the feeling isn't ingratitude and help explore what the bird-mapping week says about what Naveen truly values.

qa.q: How does Papa experience the result?
qa.a: Papa is proud and joyful, distributing sweets in the lane, likely unaware of how Naveen feels inside.

grounding: In a letter, a young adult who cleared an exam chosen by family and friends describes feeling empty after reaching it.

passage:
You want to know how it felt, Bhupen, getting the rank? Okay. Honestly.
I'm Aditi. From Class 8, Papa had a number stuck on the fridge: “Top 500.” Every uncle at every wedding asked about it. My best friend's brother got top 300, so the target became mine too.
I studied for four years. I skipped my cousin's wedding. I stopped painting completely.
The day the result came, rank 412, everyone was crying and clapping. Papa called forty people. I sat on the bathroom floor and waited to feel happy.
It didn't come. Not that day, not that week. It felt like I'd run a race someone else had entered me in.
Now I'm in a good college, and I'm fine. But the only time I've felt that deep, quiet contentment this year was painting the hostel mural last month. Nobody asked me to do that.

qa.q: What rank did Aditi get?
qa.a: Aditi got rank 412.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel on the bathroom floor on result day?
qa.a: Aditi felt empty and hollow, waiting for happiness that never came because the goal had been Papa's and the uncles', not Aditi's own.

qa.q: What could Aditi do now to find more satisfaction?
qa.a: Aditi could make regular space for painting and think about which goals truly match Aditi's own values.

qa.q: How might Papa see result day differently from Aditi?
qa.a: Papa probably felt thrilled and proud, calling forty people, without knowing Aditi felt nothing.

grounding: The monologue shows a young adult reaching a rank target set by family and feeling empty, because the goal did not match personal values.

passage:
January: Kavitha's older brother Suraj said a bank job was the safest life. “Clear the exam, and you're set.” So Kavitha studied for it every night after college, though her notebook margins filled with sketches of buildings.
August: The result came. She had cleared it. Suraj hugged her; Amma distributed sweets to the whole street. Kavitha smiled for the photos. Inside, she felt flat, as if she'd crossed someone else's finish line.
October: On her first week of training, she sat at a counter stamping forms. At lunch she walked past a new library being built next door and stood watching the architects argue over a drawing for twenty minutes.
That night she wrote in her notebook: “I got what Suraj wanted for me. I don't know yet what I want. But it's not this.”

qa.q: What did Kavitha's notebook margins fill with?
qa.a: They filled with sketches of buildings.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel when the result came, even though she had cleared it?
qa.a: She felt flat and empty, as if she had crossed someone else's finish line.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do next?
qa.a: She could explore her interest in buildings, perhaps by talking to an architect or a career counsellor, before deciding her next step.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel if he read the notebook entry?
qa.a: Suraj might feel hurt or confused, having truly believed the bank job was best for her.

grounding: The three beats show a young adult reaching a goal set by her brother and feeling empty because it did not match her own values.

passage:
Ankita, you're asking if you should do the MBA just because everyone in your batch is. Let me, your Kalyani Mashi, tell you about 1994.
I was twenty-one. My father had decided I would be a chartered accountant, like him. I passed every exam, first attempt. The day I got my final result, the whole family came to our flat in Kolkata. My father gave a speech.
I remember standing in the kitchen, holding a plate of sandesh, feeling nothing. Nothing at all. I kept thinking, Is this it?
I worked as an accountant for six years before I let myself admit I wanted to teach. When I finally did, the first day in a classroom, I felt more alive than on that whole result day.
Don't chase a finish line someone else drew for you.

qa.q: What did Kalyani hold in the kitchen on result day?
qa.a: She held a plate of sandesh.

qa.q: Why did young Kalyani feel nothing on result day?
qa.a: She felt empty because the goal had been her father's; passing it gave no real satisfaction to her own values.

qa.q: At what point in the story did Kalyani's path change?
qa.a: After six years as an accountant, when she let herself admit she wanted to teach and started in a classroom.

qa.q: How might Kalyani's father have felt on the result day?
qa.a: He likely felt proud and happy, giving a speech, without noticing his daughter felt empty.

grounding: The elder's memory shows a young woman reaching a career goal her father set and feeling empty, since it did not match her values.

passage: The result came out while Hemant was stuck at Itarsi junction, the train four hours late and the station wifi dropping every few seconds. His phone finally loaded the page: rank 212, the college his father had circled in red two years ago. Within a minute the family group filled with Papa's voice notes, Chachu's clapping hands and Mummy's long line of sweets. Hemant typed "thank you" three times and then sat on his suitcase, staring at the tracks. His friend Swati texted: "Topper!! How does it feel?" He wrote "great," deleted it, and wrote "weird." He had spent two years solving problems he never liked, for a cheer that lasted one evening. What he kept thinking about was the sketchbook he had packed away in Class 11.

qa.q: Where was Hemant when he saw his result?
qa.a: He was stuck at Itarsi junction, where his train was four hours late and the station wifi kept dropping.

qa.q: Why does Hemant feel flat instead of happy when he gets the rank?
qa.a: He feels empty and a little lost, because the target was his father's and he spent two years on problems he never liked; the cheer does not touch anything he cares about.

qa.q: What small step could help Hemant now?
qa.a: He could take a quiet evening to write down what he actually enjoys, like the sketching he dropped, and talk honestly with Swati or a counsellor before choosing his next goal.

qa.q: How might Swati read Hemant's reply of "weird"?
qa.a: Swati probably expected joy and may be surprised, but the word tells her something is off, so a good friend would ask gently what he means.

grounding: It shows a young adult reaching a rank his family set as the target and feeling empty because it does not match what he values.

passage: Devika's offer letter arrived on a Tuesday, from the consulting firm that everyone in her Pune hostel batch had been chasing since second year. Her flatmates ordered cake and made her cut it on the balcony. Her cousin Kamal called from Bengaluru. "You did it, yaar! Remember how we all said only the best get in?" Devika laughed at the right places. Later, washing the knife in the small kitchen, she noticed she felt nothing much, only tired. The work would be spreadsheets for companies she did not care about. The weekends she had spent teaching reading to kids at the basti school down the lane suddenly felt more real than the letter lying on her bed. She opened her laptop and read the offer again, waiting for the happiness to arrive.

qa.q: What did Devika's flatmates do when her offer letter came?
qa.a: They ordered cake and made her cut it on the balcony.

qa.q: How does Devika feel after the celebration, and what shows it?
qa.a: She feels tired and hollow rather than proud; she laughs on the phone with Kamal, but alone at the sink she notices she feels nothing much and keeps waiting for happiness.

qa.q: What could Devika try before she accepts the job?
qa.a: She could list what she values, like the teaching she does on weekends, and talk it through with someone she trusts, so her next choice is based on her own reasons.

qa.q: How does Kamal see Devika's news?
qa.a: To Kamal it is a clear win, proof she is among "the best", so he may not guess that she feels empty about it.

grounding: It shows a young adult reaching a goal her peers chased and finding it brings little satisfaction because it does not match what she values.

passage:
"You got in! Top dance society, Chandrika! We told you you'd make it!" Jasleen squealed, grabbing her arm outside the auditorium.
"Yeah," Chandrika said. "We did it."
"We? You did it. Three rounds of auditions!"
"You and the others picked it for me, remember? First week of college."
Jasleen stopped. "You wanted it too."
"I wanted to be with you lot." Chandrika pulled at her dupatta. "Practice is five evenings a week. That's the same time as the pottery club."
"Pottery? You went there once."
"Twice. I made a lopsided bowl and I felt calm for the first time since we came here."
"So why are you so quiet? This is huge!"
"I know it's huge. I keep waiting to feel huge."
Jasleen sat down on the steps beside her. "Okay. Tell me about the bowl." 🙂

qa.q: How many rounds of auditions did Chandrika go through?
qa.a: She went through three rounds of auditions.

qa.q: What is Chandrika feeling about getting into the dance society?
qa.a: She feels flat and uneasy; she says she keeps waiting to feel huge, because the goal was picked by her friends while pottery is what made her feel calm.

qa.q: Which choice by Jasleen helps most in this scene, and why?
qa.a: Jasleen stops cheering, sits down and asks about the bowl, which gives Chandrika room to look at what she really values instead of defending the win.

qa.q: What would change if Jasleen had kept insisting the win was huge?
qa.a: Chandrika might have hidden her empty feeling and stayed in a club that eats up the evenings she wants for pottery.

grounding: It shows a young adult reaching a target her friends set and feeling empty because it does not match what she values.

passage:
I'm Damini, and the day the results came out was Dhanteras; our whole lane was buying steel pots and lighting diyas. I'd cleared the bank PO exam. First attempt. The thing my father had talked about since I was fourteen, the thing Eshaan and my whole coaching batch had pinned on the wall.
Everyone called. My phone was hot in my hand. Mummy made kheer. I smiled at every single person and said thank you.
And then at night, on the terrace, with the diyas burning down, I waited for the feeling. The big one. It never came. It was just quiet. Like finishing someone else's homework.
Eshaan messaged: "Now you're set for life!" I typed "yes!!" and put the phone face down. I kept thinking about the evenings I'd skipped pottery class at the community centre to study reasoning. I'd liked the pottery. I never told anyone that.

qa.q: Which exam had Damini cleared?
qa.a: The bank PO exam, on the first attempt.

qa.q: What did Damini feel on the terrace that night?
qa.a: Damini felt empty and flat instead of joyful, as if the win belonged to someone else, "like finishing someone else's homework".

qa.q: What could Damini do with that empty feeling?
qa.a: Treat it as information: take time to ask what Damini actually values, perhaps go back to pottery, and talk honestly at home about what comes next instead of just typing "yes!!".

qa.q: How might Damini's father see the result?
qa.a: Damini's father has talked about it since Damini was fourteen, so the father probably feels proud and relieved, with no idea of the emptiness behind the smiles.
